title: Claude Code settings scopes, precedence and permission rules
titleVi: Phạm vi cài đặt, thứ tự ưu tiên và quy tắc phân quyền trong Claude Code

units.text: Configure Claude tools and environments for teams
What you will be able to do
Pick the right settings file for a rule that is shared with the team, kept personal, or enforced by the organization
Predict which value applies when a key is set in several scopes, and explain why permission lists merge instead of replacing each other
Write allow, ask and deny rules and predict the outcome when a broad deny and a narrow allow both match
Decide whether a team convention belongs in CLAUDE.md or in settings
Key concept
Settings scope

Each Claude Code settings file has a scope, and the scope decides who the file reaches and how much weight its values carry. Managed settings come from the organization and sit above every file a developer controls. Below them are the shared project file that the team commits, the local file that stays with one developer, and the user file that applies across one developer's projects.
In this lesson
Four settings scopes and who each one reaches
Which value wins when scopes disagree
Writing allow, ask and deny rules
Shared instructions versus enforced settings
Four settings scopes and who each one reaches

When a team uses Claude Code, the first choice for any setting is which file it goes in. The same permission rule does different things depending on where you put it. Committed to the repository, it reaches every teammate. In your home directory, it stays on your laptop. Deployed by IT, nobody below can override it. Claude Code reads four scopes, and each one answers the question "who gets this?" differently.
The four settings scopes, where each lives, and what it is for
Scope
File
Who it affects
Use it for
Managed
managed-settings.json and other managed sources
Everyone the organization deploys it to
Security policy and compliance requirements
Shared project
.claude/settings.json
Everyone working in the folder; commit it so teammates get it
Team permissions, hooks, plugins, and the environment variables the project needs
Project local
.claude/settings.local.json
You, in this one project only
Personal overrides for one project, and testing before you share
User
~/.claude/settings.json
You, in every project on this machine
Personal preferences such as theme, editor mode, default model
For a platform team, the shared project file is the one that matters.

lives in the repository, so changes to it go through ordinary code review and land in every clone on the next pull. Until you commit it, though, it is just a file on your disk and nobody else has it. A rule you write in

never leaves your machine, even if that machine is the team's reference box. Managed settings are the wrong tool for team conventions the other way round: the organization deploys them, so developers do not create or edit them, and they skip the repository's review process altogether.
The local file is where personal overrides belong. When Claude Code first writes
in a git repository, it adds the file to your global git excludes so it stays out of your commits. If you create the file by hand, add it to

yourself. Claude Code also writes to this file for you: choosing "Yes, and don't ask again" on a Bash prompt saves an allow rule here. Because the file belongs to you and not to the repository, its allow rules apply without the workspace trust step that the committed file needs, as long as the file stays untracked.
On the exam
Shared rules that go through code review belong in the committed
. Personal overrides that must never leave the machine belong in
. Managed settings are for organization policy that developers cannot change, not for team conventions.
Exam trap
Team-shared rules belong in managed-settings.json because it reaches every machine.
Why is that wrong?

Checkpoint 2 of 6
Exam question

A platform team wants every engineer's Claude Code session to inherit a shared set of Bash allow rules and MCP server configuration that the team maintains and reviews through normal code review, while still letting each engineer add personal overrides that never leave their own machine. Where should the team place the shared rules, and where should individual overrides go?
Commit the shared rules to .claude/settings.json in the project, and let engineers add personal overrides in .claude/settings.local.json
Commit the shared rules to ~/.claude/settings.json on a reference machine, and let engineers add personal overrides in .claude/settings.json
Deploy the shared rules through managed-settings.json at the OS policy path, and let engineers add overrides in .claude/settings.json
Commit the shared rules to .mcp.json only, and let engineers add their own personal overrides into ~/.claude.json

Which value wins when scopes disagree
For a single-value key such as
, the higher scope wins outright. From highest to lowest, the order is: managed settings, then JSON passed with
for one session, then project local, then shared project, then user. The
flag sits above your user, project and local files but below managed settings. It can set anything your user file can set, but never a managed key.

Arrays work differently, and permission rules are arrays. Across the non-managed scopes, Claude Code merges the arrays instead of letting the higher file replace the lower one. Suppose the project file denies a command and your local file allows something. The local file does not replace the project's deny list. Both rules end up in the effective set. A few keys are exceptions.
is an ordered chain, so Claude Code takes the whole value from the highest file that defines it. When managed settings define
, Claude Code applies that list as-is and ignores entries you add lower down.
Your user settings set
to one value and your project's shared settings set it to another. Which applies, and does the answer change for
Checkpoint 3 of 6
Check yourself

Your project's committed .claude/settings.json has a permissions.deny entry for a command. In your .claude/settings.local.json, you add a permissions.allow entry for a narrower form of that command. Local settings rank above shared project settings. What ends up in the effective permission rules?
Only your local rules, because the higher-ranked local file replaces the project's permissions arrays
Only the narrower rule, because a more specific rule replaces a broader one from another scope
Only the project's rules, because a committed file outranks a personal one for permissions
Both: the arrays merge, so your allow rule is added and the project's deny rule stays

Writing allow, ask and deny rules
A permission rule names a tool and, optionally, a specifier in parentheses.
on its own matches every Bash command.
matches only that exact command.
matches reading
in the current directory, and
matches fetches to that domain. Some tools also accept a parameter match such as
. Each rule names one parameter, so gating on two parameters takes two rules. Rules go into
or
in whichever scope should own them.
A settings file that pre-approves lint and test commands and denies reading .env files
json

The three rule types do three different jobs. An allow rule lets a tool run without asking for approval. An ask rule prompts for confirmation every time. A deny rule stops the tool from being used at all. An allow rule does not grant access past a deny; it only removes the prompt. Because rules from every scope merge into one set, a project-level
deny and a local
allow both apply to
, and the call is blocked. A more specific allow does not carve an exception out of a broad deny, and a local file does not cancel a project's deny.
Path rules hide an asymmetry that catches teams writing secret-file protections. As an allow rule,
matches only
under the current directory. As a deny or ask rule, the same pattern matches a
directory at any depth. So
in a deny list also covers nested copies such as

Predict first
A developer is prompted before Claude runs
and picks "Yes, and don't ask again". Where does that approval end up, and how long does it last?
In .claude/settings.local.json as an allow rule, permanently for this repository and command
In the shared .claude/settings.json, for the whole team
Nowhere on disk; it lasts until the session ends
Exam trap
A narrower allow rule in local settings, such as Bash(aws s3 ls), creates an exception to a broader project deny such as Bash(aws *).
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 4 of 6
Check yourself
A teammate wants Claude to run
without stopping for approval. The committed .claude/settings.json denies
. The teammate adds
to permissions.allow in their .claude/settings.local.json. What happens the next time Claude tries to run
It runs without a prompt, because the more specific allow rule makes an exception to the broad deny
Claude Code asks for confirmation, because the allow rule and the deny rule conflict
It runs without a prompt, because the local file ranks above the shared project file and overrides its deny
It is blocked, because both rules apply and the deny rule wins; an allow rule only removes the prompt
Checkpoint 5 of 6
Exam question

A security lead configures a project-level deny rule Bash(aws *) to block all AWS CLI usage from Claude Code. A developer later adds an allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls) to their local settings so they can list bucket contents. When the developer runs aws s3 ls in a session, what happens?
The command is blocked, because deny rules are evaluated before allow rules and a broad deny cannot carry allowlist exceptions from a narrower allow rule
The command runs without a prompt, because the more specific allow rule Bash(aws s3 ls) takes precedence over the broader deny pattern Bash(aws *)
The command triggers a one-time confirmation prompt, because Claude Code merges conflicting rules of equal specificity into an ask decision
The command runs without a prompt, because local settings always override project settings regardless of whether the rule is allow or deny

Shared instructions versus enforced settings
CLAUDE.md files use the same layering as settings, but they guide Claude instead of constraining it. A project
(or
) reaches team members through source control.
holds personal preferences for all projects.
holds personal notes for one project. A managed policy CLAUDE.md at the OS policy path, such as
on Linux, carries organization-wide instructions that are loaded in every session and cannot be excluded.
The split matters because an instruction is not a control. "Never read .env" written in CLAUDE.md is guidance that Claude may or may not follow.
in
stops the read regardless. If two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick either one arbitrarily, which is acceptable for style guidance but not for a security boundary.

Check yourself
Security requires that Claude Code never reads

files on any developer machine, and nobody may opt out. Someone proposes adding "Never read .env files" to the managed policy CLAUDE.md, because it loads in every session and can't be excluded. What should the organization do?
Use the managed CLAUDE.md as proposed, because an instruction that can't be excluded is enforced in every session
Put the instruction in the committed project CLAUDE.md so it goes through code review and reaches every clone
Put the instruction in both the managed CLAUDE.md and the project CLAUDE.md so the two layers reinforce each other
Add a Read(./.env) rule to permissions.deny in managed settings, because a CLAUDE.md instruction guides Claude but doesn't block the read
